A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same visual diffusion framework and three geometric tasks. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, allowing retained, relocated, and newly added material to be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on inscribed squares, Steiner trees, and maximum-area polygons in Tables 1–3, plus a regression ablation in Appendix A.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds continuous-coordinate evaluation, Steiner regression results, and learned-solver comparisons in Section 8.

M1.justification: The conditional U-Net, noise-prediction objective, 100-step diffusion procedure, square snapping, and graph/polygon extraction remain unchanged. The new regression models are comparators, and continuous-coordinate scoring changes evaluation rather than the proposed solver.

E1.justification: Both versions study the same synthetic inscribed-square, Euclidean Steiner-tree, and MaxAP tasks. Steiner evaluation still extends through 41–50 points and MaxAP through 13–15 points. The added analyses and comparators introduce no new task or input population; omitted generation details do not establish changed training data.

E2.justification: Section 8.3 adds evaluated comparisons with DIFUSCO on MaxAP and DeepSteiner on Steiner trees; both were only discussed or cited in v1. Section 8.2 also introduces regression as a Steiner-tree comparator, extending beyond the existing MaxAP regression comparison. MST and random baselines remain.

E3.justification: Section 8.1 adds float-corner squareness, point-to-polyline alignment, and a rasterized-ground-truth round-trip control. New comparisons specify matched regression training budgets and DIFUSCO best-of-10 sampling with top-n edge selection without greedy insertion. Existing main-experiment training and evaluation protocols are retained.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands validation of the central formulation: Section 8.1 investigates whether pixel-space accuracy survives continuous-coordinate evaluation and separates rasterization effects using a ground-truth control. Section 8.2 extends the diffusion-versus-regression ablation to Steiner trees. The original MaxAP ablation is retained as Table 5.

E5.justification: Mean ± standard deviation reporting and the proposed method's best-of-10 candidate sampling remain. Neither version reports independent training-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Additional result rows do not establish a changed statistical estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Tables 4 and 6–8 add substantial results, including snapped parametric alignment of -1.17 pixels and Steiner regression validity rates. Table 7 reports DIFUSCO MaxAP optimality of 75.2% versus 57.4% for ours at 7–12 points. Table 8 adds DeepSteiner's 10–20-point length ratio of 1.0355 alongside ours at 1.0008 with 99.6% validity. Existing main-table results are largely retained at reduced displayed precision.

T1.justification: The problem definitions, alignment and squareness equations, training loss, and snapping optimization are unchanged. The added stability and continuity discussion supplies an informal interpretation, without introducing a formal theorem, proof, or revised mathematical assumption.

C1.justification: Section 6 newly states that inference time remains constant regardless of input size. It also qualifies the shared-framework claim by acknowledging minimal decoding alongside task-specific training data. The central claim that standard visual diffusion approximates solutions across three geometric problems, without claiming superiority to specialized solvers, remains.

C2.justification: Section 6 adds stability and continuity arguments for tolerating quantization and explicitly leaves 3D evaluation to future work. Section 8.1 interprets discretization and prediction errors as non-compounding. Section 8.3 adds substantive tradeoffs: DIFUSCO's MaxAP quality versus the proposed framework's generality, and DeepSteiner's perfect validity versus shorter valid outputs from the proposed method.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access URL and implementation information for new comparisons. However, Section 7.1 omits v1 Appendix B.1's harmonic range, 500 angular samples, square-size and transformation ranges, 10% circle augmentation, and 100,000-example dataset size. These are documentation removals, not evidence that the underlying experiment changed.

R1.justification: The main related-work survey remains substantially unchanged. v2 adds four references concerning network stability and approximation, and Section 8.3 explicitly positions the approach against the already-cited DIFUSCO and DeepSteiner methods through their accuracy, generality, and validity tradeoffs.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose is retained. The conclusion is expanded, several captions and sentences are edited, and the appendices are reorganized: implementation details move from Appendix B to Section 7, while the former Appendix A becomes Section 8.2 within Additional Experiments.

P2.justification: v2 reformats typography, captions, headings, and page flow throughout. It adds Figure 10 and Tables 4, 6, 7, and 8; the old Table 4 becomes Table 5. Figures 7–8 gain explicit Optimal/Ours/Delta labels, Figure 9 relocates, and Figure 4 displays 24 examples rather than 32.

improvement.justification: Sections 8.1–8.3 strengthen empirical grounding through continuous-geometry validation and learned-solver comparisons, including unfavorable MaxAP findings and explicit Steiner validity tradeoffs. These gains are tempered by removal of reproducibility details from the curve-generation recipe and a stronger constant-runtime claim without timing evidence. Overall, v2 provides a better-supported assessment of the unchanged method, with a limited net quality improvement.
